clinicalPearls: Arise from parasympathetic paraganglia at the carotid body, jugulotympanic, vagal and laryngeal sites and are usually non-secretory, unlike the sympathetic abdominal and adrenal tumours
A carotid body tumour presents as a painless, slowly enlarging mass at the carotid bifurcation that is mobile from side to side but not vertically and may transmit a pulsation or bruit
Jugulotympanic tumours cause pulsatile tinnitus, conductive hearing loss and a retrotympanic reddish mass, whereas vagal tumours may cause hoarseness or lower cranial nerve palsies
A substantial proportion are hereditary, most often linked to succinate dehydrogenase (SDHx) subunit mutations, particularly SDHD and SDHB
Even when clinically silent, biochemical screening for catecholamine excess with plasma or urinary metanephrines is advised because a minority secrete, chiefly noradrenaline and normetanephrine
Cross-sectional imaging shows an intensely vascular enhancing mass with flow voids giving a salt-and-pepper appearance, and functional imaging helps detect multifocal disease
Management is individualised between surgical resection, radiotherapy and watchful surveillance depending on size, site, cranial nerve risk and genetics
SDHB carriers warrant particular vigilance because of a higher risk of malignant and metastatic behaviour
reference.pathophysiology: Head and neck paragangliomas are neuroendocrine tumours derived from paraganglia of the parasympathetic nervous system distributed along the carotid, jugulotympanic and vagal territories. In contrast to their sympathetic abdominal and adrenal counterparts, most are non-chromaffin and do not oversecrete catecholamines. A large fraction are hereditary, driven by germline mutations in succinate dehydrogenase complex subunit genes such as SDHD, SDHB, SDHC, SDHAF2 and SDHA, which impair mitochondrial complex II and stabilise hypoxia-inducible factors, promoting a pseudohypoxic, pro-angiogenic state and slow tumour growth. Chronic hypoxia, for example at high altitude, can also enlarge the carotid body. Much of the morbidity arises from local mass effect on adjacent cranial nerves and great vessels.
additionalDifferentials: Phaeochromocytoma or sympathetic abdominal and thoracic paraganglioma
Vagal or hypoglossal schwannoma or neurofibroma
Deep lobe parotid or other salivary gland tumour
Skull base meningioma at the jugular foramen
additionalInvestigations: Plasma free or 24-hour urinary metanephrines and normetanephrines to detect secretory tumours before any intervention
MRI of the neck and skull base with contrast for the characteristic vascular salt-and-pepper appearance and cranial nerve relationships
CT to define bony erosion at the skull base and jugular foramen
Somatostatin-receptor PET or metaiodobenzylguanidine imaging to identify multifocal or metastatic disease
Germline genetic testing for SDHx and related susceptibility genes with genetic counselling
Digital subtraction angiography with consideration of preoperative embolisation
redFlags: Biochemical evidence of catecholamine excess requiring alpha-adrenergic blockade before surgery or anaesthesia to avoid a hypertensive crisis
Rapid growth, pain or new lower cranial nerve palsies suggesting aggressive or malignant behaviour
Multifocal disease or a positive family history indicating a hereditary syndrome, especially SDHB, with metastatic risk
Skull base extension threatening hearing, swallowing or the airway
reference.prognosis: Most head and neck paragangliomas are slow-growing and benign, and long-term control is achievable with surgery, radiotherapy or surveillance; however cranial nerve deficits may result from the tumour or its treatment, and SDHB-related tumours carry a higher risk of metastatic spread, so lifelong follow-up is warranted.
pitfalls: Biopsying a pulsatile neck mass before excluding a vascular paraganglioma, risking haemorrhage
Proceeding to surgery without biochemical screening, precipitating an intraoperative catecholamine surge in a secretory tumour
Overlooking the strong hereditary basis and failing to offer SDHx genetic testing and family screening
Assuming unilateral single disease without imaging for synchronous multifocal tumours
references: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma
